title: 6 Leadership Problems That Aren’t What They Look Like
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Gaurav Jain, an engineering leader with twenty years of experience, opens with a story of mistaking a dependency problem for a discipline problem: when his team missed three deadlines he added check-ins and status updates, and things got worse. Using the analogy of a doctor who asks questions about a headache before treating it, he argues that the biggest blind spot in leadership is jumping from a visible symptom straight to a fix. He then walks through six common situations (a team that agrees in meetings but does nothing, a quiet top performer, slipping deadlines, silent meetings, constant escalation, and two senior people who cannot work together), listing several plausible root causes for each and a one-line takeaway. He ends with three diagnostic questions: what changed, whether it is one person or everyone, and where else the pattern shows up. The post closes with a promotion for his Kyoshi coaching tool, but the diagnostic framework stands on its own.
points: The same symptom can have very different root causes, so a fix aimed at the symptom (more meetings, more buffer, a workshop) often makes the real problem worse.
Silence in a meeting does not equal commitment; Abilene-paradox dynamics, unclear ownership and low trust can all produce polite agreement and no action.
Missed deadlines may come from the planning fallacy, too many priorities, hidden dependencies or scope creep, and padding estimates hides the delay rather than addressing it.
Empowerment cannot be demanded, since teams learn it from what happens after they decide, and escalation often traces to unclear decision rights or past overruling.
Three questions help diagnose before prescribing: what changed, is it one person or everyone, and where else does it show up.
quotes: At that point, I realized that I had mistaken a dependency problem for a discipline problem, two very different problems with very different solutions.
I find that leadership works the same way, except that most of us like to skip the questions.
Here’s what I’ve noticed and experienced after 20+ years of leading teams: the symptom is what you see or observe around you, but the root cause is what you need to fix.
Just because you didn’t hear any disagreement in a meeting, it doesn’t mean that everyone is committed to the plan.
Silence doesn’t always mean that people feel fearful of speaking up. Sometimes the problem is the room, not the people.
You can’t force empowerment. Your team learns it from what happens after they decide.
If you change the people and the conflict would still exist, then it’s a system problem, not a people problem.
When I look back at those three missed deadlines that I was talking about at the beginning, the fix wasn’t more check-ins. It was a 30-minute conversation with the other team’s manager.
